name: Tesofensine

lead: Tesofensine is an oral drug that was first tested for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Participants lost weight, so the developer turned to obesity.
A 2008 phase II trial found weight loss exceeding placebo by about 4.5% to 10.6% over 24 weeks. It has not been approved by major regulators.

paras: It blocks the reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in the brain. In animals this reduces appetite via hypothalamic circuits.

Reported effects include dry mouth, nausea, insomnia and increased heart rate and blood pressure. Related drugs such as sibutramine were withdrawn for safety reasons. It is unapproved, and supply outside trials is unregulated.

lead: Tesofensine (development code NS2330) is an investigational oral drug that blocks the reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin. It was developed by the Danish company NeuroSearch, first for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and then pursued as an obesity treatment after weight loss was observed in those trials [1][2].

In a 24-week phase II trial in 203 obese adults, published in The Lancet in 2008, placebo-adjusted weight loss ranged from about 4.5% to 10.6% across the three doses tested [3][4]. Later work combined it with metoprolol (Tesomet) in rare forms of obesity [5]. It is not approved by the US FDA or the European Medicines Agency for any use, and available reviews list it among drugs under development [6][7].

Reported adverse effects in the literature include dry mouth, nausea, insomnia and increases in heart rate and blood pressure [8]. It is discussed on looksmax.org as a weight-loss option that users source outside regulated channels [9].
infobox: Investigational; not approved by FDA or EMA

paras: No regulator has approved tesofensine. Its studied use is obesity, including in hypothalamic obesity and Prader-Willi syndrome, usually in combination with metoprolol [5][10][11].

Interest in appearance centres on fat loss and appetite suppression. Grokipedia notes attention from bodybuilding and fitness communities during cutting phases [8]. A looksmax.org thread has users asking each other about experiences with the drug [9].

Phase II trials in Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, which ran between 2003 and 2007, did not lead to approval for those conditions, but weight loss occurred in participants [1][2][12][13][14]. The dedicated obesity trial enrolled 203 participants randomized to 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks, with a diet run-in; weight loss was 4.5%, 9.2% and 10.6% greater than placebo respectively, and the authors compared this with the 3 to 5 kg usually gained over placebo by approved drugs [3][4]. A separate analysis found reduced appetite sensations with treatment [15]. A study in recreational stimulant users examined subjective and objective effects [16]. Longer-term safety and energy-balance studies were registered [17][18].

A randomized trial of Tesomet, tesofensine with metoprolol, in hypothalamic obesity was published in 2022 [5]. Smaller registered phase II studies covered type 2 diabetes, Prader-Willi syndrome and hypothalamic injury [19][10][11]. Animal studies report appetite suppression via noradrenergic and dopaminergic pathways and silencing of hypothalamic GABA neurons [20][21]. No large phase III trial results in the general obese population appear in the peer-reviewed literature reviewed here.

The phase II literature reports dry mouth, nausea, constipation, insomnia and raised heart rate and blood pressure, which reviewers cite as concerns for cardiovascular safety [8][1][22]. Reviews on centrally acting weight-loss drugs highlight that agents acting on monoamines can have neuropsychiatric effects and that earlier drugs in this space, such as sibutramine and rimonabant, were withdrawn for safety reasons [22][23].

In vitro it potently blocks reuptake of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, raising their levels in synapses [1]. Rat studies point to indirect activation of alpha-1 adrenoceptor and dopamine D1 pathways as the basis of appetite suppression [20]. A 2024 mouse study reports silencing of hypothalamic GABAergic neurons [21].

NeuroSearch developed the compound with Boehringer Ingelheim initially for neurodegenerative disease; weight loss seen in patients led it to pursue obesity [1]. Grokipedia adds that development for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's ended around 2008 and later commercial work was taken up by Saniona [8].

Tesofensine is not an authorized medicine in the US or EU, and forum users who discuss it describe obtaining it outside regulated supply [9][8]. Specific sourcing and dosing details are not provided here.
